design_detail: Systematic review with mixed-effects meta-regression updating Stockwell et al. (2016): 107 cohort studies (the 87 of 2016 plus 20 published from 2015 to 2021) with 724 relative-risk estimates for all-cause mortality by level of alcohol intake, pooled with study-level adjustment for abstainer biases and other characteristics, repeated with occasional drinkers as the reference group, and stratified by cohort median age at enrolment (under 56 versus 56 or older) and by sex. Described as preregistered on the Open Science Framework; the registration (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G, registered 3 November 2021) was read for this card.
can_establish: Whether the 2016 finding (a low-volume relative risk close to 1 after study-level adjustment) holds with 20 more studies, and how pooled estimates in the cohort literature to mid-2021 differ by cohort age and by sex.
cannot_establish: Causation; that low-volume drinking has no association with mortality (the fully adjusted interval, 0.85 to 1.01, includes a reduction of up to 15%); the risk in any defined population (the adjusted estimates are study-level model predictions at unstated covariate values); outcomes other than all-cause mortality; or precise sex-specific risks at heavier intake in women, which rest on 11 to 17 studies.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed and Web of Science for studies published from January 1980 to 31 July 2021, stated to be regardless of language, plus reference lists of earlier meta-analyses; staff of the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA) ran a preliminary search (Abstract › Data Sources; Methods, 2nd paragraph; Article Information). Flow chart and search details in Supplement 1 (eFigure 1, eAppendix; not read). The registration describes the new search as covering 1 July 2016 to 30 June 2021 and requires English-language publication (registry record).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cohort studies of alcohol consumption and all-cause mortality; details in the eAppendix (not read). The registration specifies original peer-reviewed cohort studies in English, any age, sex, ethnicity or location, reporting at least three levels of daily consumption, and excludes cohorts selected for illness or for heavy, problematic or dependent drinking.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (counts of studies, some counted more than once): published 1980 to 2004, 51; 2005 to 2014, 36; 2015 to 2021, 20. Median age at enrolment 19 to 55 in 67, 56 to 78 in 46. Men only 73, women only 48, men and women 31. North and Central America 41, Europe and Australia 53, Asia 14. Follow-up 3.7 to 10.5 years in 45, 11 to 41 years in 62. Primary studies controlled for smoking in 91, socio-economic status in 69, body-mass index in 61, diet in 17.
sample.selection_effects: The 87 earlier studies come from an English-only search ending in December 2014. The paper says the update was made regardless of language, but the registration requires English. The registered search starts on 1 July 2016, and the paper does not say how studies published between January 2015 and June 2016 were found (at least two of the 20 new studies, refs 14 and 15, appeared in 2015 and in the first 2016 issue of their journal). Cohorts are mostly from high-income countries.

exposure.measurement: Mean daily intake in grams of ethanol as reported or converted from each study's categories with country-specific drink definitions where not stated (refs 33 and 34; the registration lists, for example, 8 g per UK unit, 13.45 g per Canadian and 14 g per US drink); self-report in all primary studies (Methods, 3rd paragraph; registry record).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Categories: lifetime abstainers (reference), former drinkers (now completely abstaining), occasional more than 0 and under 1.3 g/day (under 9.1 g a week), low volume 1.3 to 24.0 g/day (1.30 to under 25 in the tables), medium 25 to 44, high 45 to 64, highest 65 g/day or more (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 2). The Key Points equate under 25 g/day with about two Canadian standard drinks. For orientation, 25 g/day is 175 g/week (editors' arithmetic).
exposure.polysubstance: Whether the primary study controlled for smoking is a study-level covariate; no other substance considered.

comparison.controls: Abstainers as defined in each study: 21 of 107 studies used strictly defined lifetime abstainers (zero consumption or never one drink); 50 included both former and occasional drinkers, 28 former drinkers only and 8 occasional drinkers only (Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1). Table 2 repeats the analysis with occasional drinkers as the reference.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Fully adjusted model, study-level covariates: abstainer biases, median age, sex, country, publication year, follow-up years, drinking pattern, and whether the study controlled for heart problems, social status, race, diet, exercise, body-mass index and smoking (Table 2, footnote c). The registration describes candidate selection by univariate p < 0.20, change in estimate and collinearity checks.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Within the cohorts, earlier drinking history, reasons for abstaining, earlier health, socio-economic position and lifestyle are handled only by whatever each study adjusted for; the meta-regression codes whether such adjustment was made, not its adequacy.

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality relative risks (hazard ratios or rate ratios) from each cohort, log-transformed; variance from reported standard errors, confidence intervals or numbers of deaths (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Death is an objective outcome; ascertainment in the cohorts is not described.
outcomes.operationalization: RR for each drinking category against the study's reference group. The ‘unadjusted’ column is an unweighted mean of log RRs; ‘partially adjusted’ is weighted and allows for between-study variation; ‘fully adjusted’ adds the study-level covariates (Table 2 footnotes).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One outcome, estimated for eight rows at three levels of adjustment and two reference groups (Table 2), then in age and sex strata (Tables 3 and 4) and a young-cohort subgroup (eTable 3), each by t test at .05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Three coders (J. Z., F. A., J. C.) extracted and coded data independently (Methods, 3rd paragraph). The registration states that those who searched for studies were unaware of the hypotheses and that coders were blind to each other's coding.

analysis.effect_sizes: All RRs for all-cause mortality, unadjusted / partially adjusted / fully adjusted, against lifetime nondrinkers as modelled (Table 2): former drinkers 1.22 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.33) / 1.17 (1.08 to 1.26) / 1.26 (1.12 to 1.42), 28 studies, 56 estimates; occasional 0.92 (0.84 to 1.01) / 0.89 (0.83 to 0.95) / 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06), 24 studies; low volume 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88) / 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88) / 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01), 99 studies, 306 estimates; medium 1.02 (0.96 to 1.08) / 0.97 (0.92 to 1.02) / 1.05 (0.96 to 1.14); high 1.07 (0.99 to 1.16) / 1.11 (1.03 to 1.21) / 1.19 (1.07 to 1.32); highest 1.35 (1.26 to 1.46) / 1.24 (1.16 to 1.32) / 1.35 (1.23 to 1.47); current (active) drinkers 0.97 / 0.93 / 1.02 (0.93 to 1.13). Occasional drinkers as reference, fully adjusted: abstainers 1.04 (0.94 to 1.16); low 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); medium 1.09 (0.96 to 1.25); high 1.24 (1.07 to 1.44); highest 1.41 (1.23 to 1.61); former 1.31 (1.13 to 1.52). Age strata, fully adjusted (Table 3): low volume 0.93 (0.86 to 1.01) under 56 and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.02) at 56 or older; high 1.24 (1.10 to 1.40) and 1.15 (1.02 to 1.30); highest 1.38 (1.23 to 1.55) and 1.32 (1.18 to 1.47). Sex strata, fully adjusted (Table 4): men low 0.94 (0.88 to 1.01), medium 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10), high 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), highest 1.34 (1.23 to 1.47); women low 0.99 (0.90 to 1.10), medium 1.21 (1.08 to 1.36), high 1.34 (1.11 to 1.63), highest 1.61 (1.44 to 1.80); current female drinkers 1.03 (0.92 to 1.15); any female drinkers including former 1.22 (1.02 to 1.46). Heterogeneity Q (723 df) = 5314.80, I2 above 85.87% in every category; no publication bias by funnel plot or Egger test.
analysis.covariates: Study-level only (Table 2, footnote c); the Figure shows the low-volume RR after removing each covariate or covariate set (values not extracted). The paper does not state at which covariate values (reference levels or averages) the adjusted category RRs are evaluated; Table 1's reference categories for its bivariable tests (for example Asian cohorts, follow-up of 3.7 to 10.5 years, publication 2015 to 2021, median age 56 to 78) show that such choices are not neutral.
analysis.preregistration_detail: OSF Preregistration doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G, registered 3 November 2021 (the paper's reference 11 gives https://osf.io/tnhd3/, an author's OSF profile page that links to it). It was registered after the search ended (30 June or 31 July 2021) and, by the paper's own dates, after analysis began (September 2021), although the registration says no analyses for the new plan had been run and that the patterns relevant to hypotheses 1 to 3 were already known from the earlier dataset. Registered but not reported in the paper, with no deviation noted: hypothesis 5 (studies with lifetime drinking measures); a meta-analysis restricted to studies with lifetime abstainers; the strict subset recruited before 46 and followed to 60 or older; strata by Caucasian population and by control for heart health; CHD mortality, a registered outcome. The young-cohort subgroup was redefined (registered: recruited under 55 and followed to 55 or older, or under 45 and followed to 60 or older; reported: recruited at 50 or younger and followed to 60). The registration requires English-language studies; the paper says regardless of language.
analysis.selective_reporting: Registered analyses missing as listed above. The low-volume estimate for the 21 studies with lifetime abstainers, the analogue of the 2016 paper's key stratified result, is not given in the main text. The young-cohort subgroup is reported only in words in the main text (eTable 3, not read).
analysis.power: Women's heavier-drinking categories rest on 11 to 17 studies; occasional drinkers on 24 studies (57 estimates). The authors argue that two estimates per covariate suffice for linear regression (Limitations, 2nd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With 20 more studies the 2016 pattern recurred, with a point estimate further from 1: low-volume RR 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88) unweighted, 0.86 (0.83 to 0.88) weighted and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01) fully adjusted; occasional drinkers 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06); former drinkers 1.26; 45 to 64 g/day 1.19 and 65 g/day or more 1.35. Against occasional drinkers the fully adjusted low-volume RR was 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11). Fully adjusted low-volume estimates were identical in younger and older cohorts (0.93). Risk at 25 to 44 g/day was raised in women (1.21) but not in men (1.01).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points conclude: “Low-volume alcohol drinking was not associated with protection against death from all causes.” Gaps: (1) the fully adjusted low-volume RR is 0.93 with an upper limit of 1.01 (P = .07 in the text, .08 in Table 2), which is compatible with a reduction of up to 15%; the Discussion itself calls it a nonsignificant protective association, so the Key Points overstate a borderline null result as an absence of association; (2) the models are presented as prespecified and the protocol as preregistered, but the registration post-dates the search and the stated start of analysis, acknowledges prior knowledge of the main patterns, and planned analyses the paper does not report; (3) the abstract's statement that female drinkers had larger mortality risks (RR 1.22) uses the ‘any drinker’ row, which includes former drinkers; for current female drinkers the RR was 1.03 (0.92 to 1.15), and the excess is confined to 25 g/day or more; (4) the Discussion says risk was increased from 25 g/day, which holds for women but not for the pooled estimate (1.05, 0.96 to 1.14) or for men; (5) the abstract does not say that the adjusted estimates are study-level model predictions. The Discussion and Limitations do describe the dependence of results on modelling choices and the weakness of self-reported intake.

timeline.event: Stockwell et al.: the 87-study review this paper updates, fully adjusted low-volume RR 0.97 (0.88 to 1.07) (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round), followed in 2016 by commentaries, a critical letter from Barrett-Connor and co-signatories and the authors' replies.
Zhao et al.: CHD mortality meta-analysis by the same group, described in this paper's introduction as showing no significant cardioprotection in young cohorts followed to older age (not read).
Naimi et al.: paper on selection biases across the life course, named in the registration as the hypothesis this update tests (not read).
Wood et al. pooled analysis of current drinkers, not among the included studies (card sc_wood_2018, this round).
OSF preregistration, 3 November 2021 (doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G), read for this card.
Biddinger et al. Mendelian randomization study in UK Biobank, cited in the introduction as finding no cardioprotection (carded in this round by another reader).

This paper, and its correction (JAMA Netw Open 6:e2315283; doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.15283): incorrect 95% CIs in the Figure and the Supplement were corrected; the text and tables were not listed as changed (read).

Stockley, Hendriks and Ellison, ‘ISFAR Reiterates Its Defense of Moderate Alcohol Consumption's Health Benefits’ (J Stud Alcohol Drugs 85:136–140), listed on PubMed as a comment on this paper (not read).
Stockwell et al. review of study characteristics that may bias low-volume mortality estimates, on the project list (not read).

replication.where_it_stands: An update by the authors of the 2016 review on largely the same studies, so it does not replicate that review independently. Its adjusted low-volume estimate (0.93, 0.85 to 1.01) is closer to a protective association than the 2016 estimate and its interval touches 1, so it supports ‘no detectable net reduction’ rather than ‘no association’. It was funded partly through the process that produced Canada's guidance on alcohol and health, and it has drawn a published critique from ISFAR (2024, not read).

funding.funder: Partly funded by the Canadian Centre on Substance Use and Addiction (CCSA) as a subcontract for a Health Canada grant to develop guidance for Canadians on alcohol and health; the larger guidance project contributed some funds. Health Canada had no role in the study; CCSA staff ran a preliminary literature search but did not take part in inclusion decisions, coding, analysis, interpretation or approval of the manuscript (Article Information › Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor; Additional Contributions).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Dr Stockwell reported personal fees from the Ontario Public Servants Employees Union for expert witness testimony and personal fees from Alko outside the submitted work. Dr Sherk reported grants from the CCSA during the conduct of the study. No other disclosures.
funding.affiliations_note: Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research, University of Victoria; Department of Psychology, University of Portsmouth. The co-chairs of Canada's guidance development process are acknowledged. Zhao, Stockwell and Naimi wrote the 2016 review being updated, and Stockwell and Naimi the 2015 editorial arguing that protective effects had collapsed (card sc_chikritzhs_2015). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant analysis of cohorts recruited in early adulthood with lifetime drinking histories, strictly defined lifetime abstainers and former drinkers reassigned to the levels they drank, with common adjustment and sex-specific estimates, run to a protocol registered before the data are assembled; or a long-term randomized trial of low-volume drinking against abstention.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Cohort populations, intake level, lifetime abstainers or occasional drinkers as comparators, all-cause mortality.

An OSF preregistration with hypotheses, search, criteria, coding of biases and an analysis plan exists, but it was registered after the search was completed and after the stated start of analysis, with the main patterns admittedly known; deviations (unreported registered analyses, redefined subgroups, language) are not acknowledged in the paper.
Cohort studies chosen to compare studies with and without controls for abstainer biases (Abstract › Study Selection).

Two databases and reference lists; no grey literature, registries or expert consultation beyond a preliminary search by funder staff; the search strategy is only in the eAppendix (not read). The paper says regardless of language, but the registration requires English and the 87 carried-over studies come from an English-only search, without justification; the registered search window starts on 1 July 2016, leaving the capture of 2015 to mid-2016 publications unexplained.
Provisional: the article refers selection details to the eAppendix (not read); the registration plans two reviewers for titles and abstracts and three investigators for eligibility.
Three coders extracted and coded data independently (Methods, 3rd paragraph).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list in the article; the listed supplement contents (eAppendix, eFigures 1 to 4, eTables 1 to 3) include a flow chart but no list of excluded studies; the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the article gives aggregate characteristics only (Table 1); eTable 1 describes the 20 new studies and the 87 earlier ones are described in the 2016 paper's appendix; neither supplement was read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No formal tool; each study coded for abstainer biases, exclusion or control of baseline illness, follow-up, cohort age, intake measure and control for smoking, socio-economic status, race, diet, exercise and body-mass index; selection of reported results not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Inverse-variance-weighted mixed models with a random study effect, as registered. Met on balance, a close call: the ‘unadjusted’ column is an unweighted mean, correlation between categories sharing a reference group is handled only by the random effect, whether the most-adjusted primary estimates were used is not stated, and adjusted RRs are evaluated at unstated covariate values.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Bias covariates in the meta-regression, removal of each covariate (Figure), and age and sex strata.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion interprets the shift between unadjusted and adjusted estimates as the effect of abstainer and selection biases and says results depend on the modelling strategy.
Q and I2 reported (I2 above 85.87% in every category) and sources explored by meta-regression and strata; discussion of its impact is brief.
Funnel plot and Egger tests for each study group, all P > .05 (eFigure 2, eTable 2, not read; result stated in the text).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the funder's role and individual disclosures are stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items fail (item 4, a search restricted in practice to English without justification and with an unexplained gap in its window; item 7, no list of excluded studies), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2; items 5 and 8 are provisional (supplement not read) but non-critical and cannot change the rating. Beyond AMSTAR, the late registration and unreported registered analyses weaken the claim that the main models were prespecified. The card may be cited for the pooled estimates by intake category with their reference groups, for the elevated risk of former drinkers and of drinkers of 45 g/day or more, and for women's elevated risk from 25 g/day. It should not be cited for an absence of association at low volume, for the female ‘any drinker’ estimate as a risk of current drinking, or for any adjusted RR as the risk in a real population.

key_findings.finding: 107 cohort studies (87 from Stockwell et al., 2016, and 20 new) contributed 724 relative-risk estimates from 4,838,825 participants with 425,564 deaths; search of PubMed and Web of Science to 31 July 2021.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The search covered January 1980 to July 2021 (abstract); by the reference list, the earliest included studies are from 1981 (refs 79, 110 and 122) and two are cited with 2022 print issues (refs 30 and 31).

key_findings.finding: Reference groups: 21 studies (220 estimates) used strictly defined lifetime abstainers; 50 (265 estimates) included former and occasional drinkers among abstainers, 28 (177) former drinkers only and 8 (62) occasional drinkers only.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: By the reference lists, 14 of the 87 earlier studies are now classed as bias-free and 8 as occasional-bias only, against 13 and 9 in the 2016 paper (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted mean RR of any drinking (including former drinkers) by study characteristic: studies with lifetime abstainers only 1.19 (1.12 to 1.25) against 0.98 (0.92 to 1.04) for studies with both biases; follow-up of 11 to 41 years 1.12 (1.07 to 1.16) against 0.98 (0.92 to 1.03) for 3.7 to 10.5 years; baseline illness excluded or controlled 1.12 (1.07 to 1.17) against 1.01 (0.97 to 1.06); no control for socio-economic status 1.16 (1.10 to 1.22) against 1.01 (0.97 to 1.06) with control; quantity-frequency intake measure 1.18 (1.12 to 1.25) against 1.01 (0.97 to 1.05).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: No evidence of publication bias (funnel plot; Egger tests, all P > .05); significant heterogeneity in every drinking category (Q with 723 df = 5314.80, P < .001; I2 above 85.87%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Against lifetime nondrinkers as modelled, fully adjusted: occasional drinkers (under 1.3 g/day) RR 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06); low volume (1.3 to under 25 g/day) 0.93 (0.85 to 1.01); medium (25 to 44) 1.05 (0.96 to 1.14); high (45 to 64) 1.19 (1.07 to 1.32); highest (65 or more) 1.35 (1.23 to 1.47); former drinkers 1.26 (1.12 to 1.42). Unadjusted, low volume was 0.85 (0.81 to 0.88) and former drinkers 1.22 (1.11 to 1.33), against abstainers as defined in each study.
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers From Meta-analysis of Pooled Studies, 1st paragraph; Table 2, upper panel
key_findings.note: The low-volume P value is .07 in the abstract and text and .08 in Table 2.

key_findings.finding: With occasional drinkers as the reference, fully adjusted: abstainers RR 1.04 (0.94 to 1.16); low volume 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); medium 1.09 (0.96 to 1.25); high 1.24 (1.07 to 1.44); highest 1.41 (1.23 to 1.61); former drinkers 1.31 (1.13 to 1.52).
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers From Meta-analysis of Pooled Studies, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, lower panel

key_findings.finding: Removing study-level covariates from the fully adjusted model mostly lowered the low-volume RR, that is, moved it towards apparent protection.
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers From Meta-analysis of Pooled Studies, 1st paragraph; Figure caption
key_findings.note: The Figure is an image and its values were not extracted; its 95% CIs were corrected in May 2023.

key_findings.finding: Cohort median age interacted with mortality risk (P = .02). Fully adjusted, low-volume RR was 0.93 (0.86 to 1.01) in cohorts with median age under 56 and 0.93 (0.85 to 1.02) at 56 or older, although unadjusted it was 0.88 (0.84 to 0.93) and 0.79 (0.74 to 0.84); high volume 1.24 (1.10 to 1.40) and 1.15 (1.02 to 1.30); highest 1.38 (1.23 to 1.55) and 1.32 (1.18 to 1.47). In cohorts recruited at 50 or younger and followed to 60, RRs were higher for all drinking groups against lifetime abstainers and significant except for low volume.
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk on the Basis of Median Age of Study Cohorts at Baseline; Table 3
key_findings.note: The young-cohort subgroup values are only in eTable 3 (not read); the subgroup is defined differently in the Introduction, Results and Discussion.

key_findings.finding: Sex interacted with risk (P = .001). Fully adjusted, against lifetime nondrinkers of the same sex: men, low volume 0.94 (0.88 to 1.01), medium 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10), high 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), highest 1.34 (1.23 to 1.47); women, low volume 0.99 (0.90 to 1.10), medium 1.21 (1.08 to 1.36), high 1.34 (1.11 to 1.63), highest 1.61 (1.44 to 1.80). For women, any drinking including former drinkers 1.22 (1.02 to 1.46), current drinking 1.03 (0.92 to 1.15).
key_findings.locator: Results › All-Cause Mortality Risk for Drinkers by Sex; Table 4

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: imperfect, mostly under-reported intake, often measured once; unreliable classification of lifetime abstainers, so that risks relative to presumed lifetime abstainers may be underestimated; few studies in some strata; binge drinking not controllable; all-cause mortality only.

Correction (JAMA Netw Open 2023;6:e2315283, doi 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.15283): incorrect 95% CIs were shown in the Figure and the Supplement, and the article was corrected. The numbers on this card come from the text and Tables 1 to 4, which the notice does not list as changed.
key_findings.locator: Errors in Figure and Supplement, single paragraph

key_findings.finding: The OSF preregistration (registered 3 November 2021) states five hypotheses, an English-language inclusion criterion, a new search from 1 July 2016 to 30 June 2021 having found 31 new cohort studies, and planned analyses including studies with lifetime drinking measures, studies with lifetime abstainers only, a strict subset recruited before 46 and followed to 60 or older, and strata by sex, age, ethnicity and control for heart health, for all-cause and CHD mortality; it says no analyses for the plan had been run and that the patterns for hypotheses 1 to 3 were already known from the earlier dataset.
key_findings.locator: OSF Preregistration doi 10.17605/OSF.IO/PF95G (https://osf.io/pf95g): Study Information › Hypotheses; Design Plan › Study design; Sampling Plan › Explanation of existing data; Analysis Plan › Statistical models

reporting_issues.issue: P values differ between places: low volume, fully adjusted, P = .07 (abstract, text) against .08 (Table 2); any drinking in women P = .03 (abstract, text) against .04 (Table 4); abstainers against occasional drinkers P = .44 (text) against .45 (Table 2). The abstract gives the low-volume RR without its interval.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results; Tables 2 and 4
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the abstract alone hides that the interval reaches 1.01.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 study counts exceed 107 in most rows (median age 67 + 46 = 113; sex 73 + 48 + 31 = 152; countries 108; smoking control 109), with percentages computed on those totals; the text's sex lists name 39 + 33 + 8 + 30 = 110 studies, only 105 distinct, with refs 13, 21, 26, 29 and 84 in two lists and refs 60 and 131 in none (editors' count).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; Results › Characteristics of Included Studies, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The composition of the sex strata cannot be reconstructed from the article; study counts per stratum should be taken from Table 4.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 counts 436 and 281 estimates for the two age strata (717 in all), whereas Table 1 gives 438 and 286 (724) (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Seven estimates are unaccounted for in the age-stratified models.

reporting_issues.issue: Labels: Table 2 heads all three columns ‘Reference group = lifetime nondrinker’, although the unadjusted and partially adjusted estimates are against abstainers as defined in each study (most not lifetime abstainers), as the text says; in its lower panel rows are labelled ‘vs abstainer’ under the occasional-drinker reference; Table 4's first column is headed by median age though it is stratified by sex.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take the unadjusted 0.85 as a comparison with lifetime abstainers; cite it as against study-defined abstainers.

reporting_issues.issue: The young-cohort subgroup is defined three ways: recruited before median age 51 and followed to median age 60 or more (Introduction), recruited at 50 or younger and followed to 60 (Results), enrolled at 50 or younger and followed for at least 10 years (Discussion); the registration specified other cut-offs.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Results › Median Age; Discussion, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup result, already available only in a supplement, cannot be attributed to a defined set of studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper states the protocol was preregistered and the models prespecified, and dates the analysis from September 2021, but the cited registration was made on 3 November 2021, after the search, and itself says no analyses had yet been run; the reference given (https://osf.io/tnhd3/) opens an author's profile page rather than the registration.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 1st paragraph; Abstract; reference 11; registry record
reporting_issues.consequence: The degree of prespecification cannot be taken at face value; claims should not describe the main models as preregistered without this qualification.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper says studies were sought regardless of language, but the registration requires English-language publication and describes the combined sample as close to all such studies ever published in English.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 2nd paragraph; registry record (Design Plan › Inclusion criteria; Sampling Plan › Sample size rationale)
reporting_issues.consequence: The review should be treated as English-only.

reporting_issues.issue: The interaction of cohort age with risk is reported as F601 = 2.93, P = .02, with a single degrees-of-freedom value; F(1, 601) = 2.93 gives P of about .09, whereas P = .02 fits 4 numerator degrees of freedom (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Median Age, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the test cannot be checked as printed.
